According to the FIGO system for ovarian cancer, the stages are numbered I (1), II (2), III (3), and IV (4), each with substages:
- Stage 1A: Cancer in one ovary; capsule intact; no cancer on outer surface; no cancer cells in ascites or washings.
- Stage 1B: Cancer in both ovaries; capsules intact; no cancer on outer surface; no cancer cells in ascites or washings.
- Stage 1C: Cancer in one or both ovaries with one or more of: 1C1 (surgical spill), 1C2 (capsule rupture before surgery or cancer on outer surface), 1C3 (cancer cells in ascites or washings).
- Stage 2A: Cancer in one or both ovaries with growth/spread to uterus and/or fallopian tubes.
- Stage 2B: Cancer in one or both ovaries with growth/spread to other pelvic organs/tissues (e.g., bladder, colon, rectum).
- Stage 3A1: Cancer in one or both ovaries with spread to retroperitoneal lymph nodes; 3A1(i) ≤10 mm, 3A1(ii) >10 mm.
- Stage 3A2: Microscopic spread to abdominal lining; may include retroperitoneal lymph nodes.
- Stage 3B: Visible cancer on abdominal lining ≤2 cm; may include retroperitoneal lymph nodes.
- Stage 3C: Visible cancer on abdominal lining >2 cm; may include retroperitoneal lymph nodes or spread to liver/spleen surface.
- Stage 4A: Cancer cells in fluid around lungs (malignant pleural effusion).
- Stage 4B: Spread to inside liver/spleen, distant lymph nodes, or other organs outside abdomen.

per_example.pred_answer: Diagnostic methods for primary CNS lymphoma include: (1) MRI – most useful imaging technique for identifying PCNSL, showing brain/spine soft tissues and tumor features; (2) CT – alternative if MRI is unavailable or not recommended, using x-rays to create 3D images; (3) stereotactic biopsy – standard method to confirm diagnosis by removing a tissue sample, especially for hard-to-reach or vital areas; (4) lumbar puncture – removes cerebrospinal fluid to test for cancer cells and help confirm diagnosis and plan treatment; (5) vitrectomy – eye procedure that can sometimes confirm diagnosis without brain biopsy; (6) thorough eye exam – required for all diagnosed patients to check for lymphoma in the eyes; and (7) additional post-diagnosis tests such as blood tests, HIV test, and imaging of chest, abdomen, pelvis, and possibly bone marrow and testicles to determine extent of disease.

per_example.pred_answer:
According to the AJCC TNM system as described in the passages, colon cancer is staged as follows:
- Stage 0: Abnormal cells are on the innermost layer of the colon wall (mucosa); may become cancer and spread deeper. Also called carcinoma in situ.
- Stage 1: Cancer has grown into the second or third layer of the colon wall. No cancer in nearby lymph nodes or outside the colon.
- Stage 2: Cancer has grown into or beyond the fourth layer of the colon wall. No cancer in nearby lymph nodes or outside the colon.
- Stage 3: Cancer has spread from the colon to nearby lymph nodes, or there are tumor deposits (small tumors in the fat around the colon).
- Stage 4: Cancer has spread to areas outside the colon and nearby lymph nodes, most often to the liver and/or lungs.

The TNM system uses T (how far the tumor has grown into or through the colon wall), N (whether nearby lymph nodes have cancer), and M (whether cancer has metastasized outside the colon). These scores are combined to assign one of the stages: 0, I, II, III, or IV.

per_example.question: What is the clinical significance of tumor grade in breast cancer, and how is it assessed?
per_example.gold: Tumor grade in breast cancer, described as GX, G1, G2, or G3, reflects how abnormal the tumor cells appear microscopically and helps predict disease aggressiveness and guide management.
per_example.pred_answer: In breast cancer, tumor grade describes how abnormal the tumor cells look under a microscope (histology). Higher-grade cancers tend to grow and spread faster than lower-grade cancers. It is clinically significant because it helps predict prognosis: a low-grade tumor (G1) has a low risk of recurrence, while a high-grade tumor (G3) has a higher risk of recurrence. Grade is assessed by a pathologist who examines the tissue sample under a microscope, comparing cancer cells to normal cells; grades range from GX (cannot be determined), G1 (low), G2 (intermediate), to G3 (high).

per_example.question: What are the most common therapies used in the systemic treatment of breast cancer, and when are they indicated?
per_example.gold: Systemic therapies for breast cancer include chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, HER2-targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and targeted inhibitors, which are indicated for invasive and metastatic disease based on biomarker status.
per_example.pred_answer: The most common systemic therapies for breast cancer are chemotherapy, HER2-targeted therapy, inhibitors (CDK4/6, mTOR, PARP, PIK3CA), immunotherapy, and endocrine therapy. They are indicated based on estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2 expression; endocrine therapy for hormone receptor-positive disease, HER2-targeted therapy for HER2-positive disease, PARP inhibitors for BRCA1/2-mutated HER2-negative disease, and PIK3CA inhibitors for PIK3CA-mutated cancers. Systemic therapy is used before surgery to shrink the tumor (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), and for inflammatory breast cancer it is given first to shrink the tumor, followed by surgery and radiation.

per_example.question: How are imaging and biopsy utilized throughout the continuum of breast cancer care, from screening to diagnosis and surveillance?
per_example.gold: Imaging (mammogram, ultrasound, MRI, CT, PET) is used for screening, diagnosis, staging, and surveillance, while biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis and biomarker testing, and both are essential across all stages of breast cancer care.
per_example.pred_answer:
Imaging and biopsy are utilized throughout the breast cancer care continuum as follows:

- **Screening:** Imaging (mammograms, including 2D/3D) is used for routine screening in asymptomatic individuals. If an abnormal area is found, diagnostic mammograms are performed for closer evaluation.
- **Diagnosis:** Imaging can occur before, during, or after a biopsy. Before: imaging may determine if a biopsy is necessary. During: imaging (mammogram, ultrasound, MRI) guides the biopsy needle to the tumor (e.g., stereotactic or ultrasound-guided needle biopsy). After: imaging assesses the size and location of the cancer to help plan treatment. Biopsy removes tissue or fluid samples for pathological examination to confirm cancer and determine hormone receptor and HER2 status.
- **Staging and Treatment Planning:** Results from imaging studies and biopsy are used together to stage the cancer and determine the treatment plan. Imaging shows the primary tumor, its size, location, and whether the cancer has spread (metastasized).
- **Surveillance:** After treatment, imaging is used to check how well treatment worked and to monitor for cancer recurrence. Surveillance imaging includes CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast, or CT of the chest without contrast and MRI of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast. Biopsy is not routinely used for surveillance unless a suspicious finding requires confirmation.

**To all residents, especially older adults with fair skin, light hair, or light eyes:**

Our community has seen a rise in diagnoses of basal cell carcinoma (BCC), the most common type of skin cancer. BCC is highly treatable and curable when caught early, but it can cause serious damage if ignored. The following evidence-based guidance from clinical experts can help you protect yourself and your loved ones.

**Why is this happening?**  
BCC is caused by exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun or tanning beds. UV radiation damages the DNA inside basal skin cells, causing them to grow out of control. Risk increases with age because sun exposure builds up over time, but skin cancer is also becoming more common in younger people.

**Who is at highest risk?**  
- People with fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color  
- Older adults with many years of sun exposure  
- Anyone with a personal or family history of skin cancer  
- People who have had radiation therapy, especially at a young age  
- People with weakened immune systems (e.g., from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases)  
- People who use indoor tanning beds or spend long periods in the sun without protection

**Prevention: What you can do**  
- Avoid UV radiation from the sun and tanning beds.  
- Seek shade, wear protective clothing, and use sunscreen.  
- Do not use indoor tanning machines—they increase the risk of all skin cancers.  
- Between doctor visits, prevention is important. Regular self-checks and professional skin exams help.

In lighter skin, BCC may look like:  
- Flat, pale or yellow areas, like a scar  
- Red patches that might be itchy  
- Small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas  
- Open sores that don’t heal, might bleed, or go away and come back  

In darker skin, BCC can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border, sometimes mistaken for a normal mole.  
Look out for any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths. Skin cancer is easier to cure when caught early.

- If you notice a concerning lesion, see your doctor promptly. Testing—including a skin biopsy—is needed to diagnose BCC.  
- Surgery is the most common treatment and is usually curative. In some cases, radiation therapy or systemic therapy may be used.

per_example.question: Imagine you are a neuro-oncology fellow. Write a detailed initial diagnostic workup and staging plan for a 62-year-old patient presenting with progressive leg weakness, memory problems, and blurry vision, suspected of having primary CNS lymphoma. Your plan should outline all relevant assessments and justify their use.
per_example.gold:
For a 62-year-old patient presenting with progressive leg weakness, memory problems, and blurry vision, the initial diagnostic workup for suspected primary CNS lymphoma should include:

1. Neurological examination to assess the extent of neurological deficits and establish a clinical baseline.
2. MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast as the most sensitive imaging modality to identify CNS lesions characteristic of lymphoma.
3. Eye examination using slit lamp and potentially vitrectomy if ocular involvement is suspected, given the blurry vision.
4. Stereotactic biopsy of the brain lesion to obtain histopathologic confirmation, as this is the standard diagnostic procedure.
5. Laboratory assessments including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, and HIV and hepatitis B testing to evaluate for risk factors and baseline organ function.
6. Lumbar puncture to analyze cerebrospinal fluid for malignant cells, especially given the possibility of CSF involvement in primary CNS lymphoma.
7. Performance status evaluation to guide further diagnostic and treatment decisions.
This comprehensive approach ensures accurate diagnosis, detection of disease extent (including possible eye and CSF involvement), and risk factor assessment to inform treatment planning.

per_example.question: As a hematologist, develop a comprehensive induction and consolidation treatment plan for a newly diagnosed immunocompetent adult with primary CNS lymphoma confined to the brain. The plan should detail drug regimens, rationale, and supportive care measures.
per_example.gold:
For an immunocompetent adult with newly diagnosed primary CNS lymphoma confined to the brain, the treatment plan consists of:

Induction Phase: Initiate high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy, as this is the mainstay of induction for primary CNS lymphoma. Combine with rituximab, the primary immunotherapy agent, to enhance response. Consider adding agents such as temozolomide or vincristine as per protocol and patient tolerance. Supportive corticosteroids may be used to reduce cerebral edema and symptoms.

Consolidation Phase: Upon achieving remission or maximal response, proceed to consolidation with whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), which is the most commonly used radiation technique in this context. Alternatively, high-dose chemotherapy followed by hematopoietic stem cell rescue may be considered based on patient performance status and institutional protocols.

Throughout treatment, provide supportive care to manage symptoms and treatment side effects, involving a multidisciplinary team as needed. Monitor performance status regularly to adjust therapy and consider clinical trial participation if available.

Public Health Advisory: Primary Central Nervous System Lymphoma (PCNSL)

Primary CNS lymphoma is a rare but aggressive cancer that originates from lymphocytes within the central nervous system, most commonly affecting the brain but also the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and eyes. Individuals at increased risk include those with impaired immune systems, such as patients with immunodeficiency disorders, HIV infection, Epstein-Barr virus, autoimmune diseases, organ transplants, and older adults.

Key symptoms to watch for include leg or arm weakness, difficulties with coordination or movement, changes in personality or behavior, memory problems, headaches, nausea, vomiting, seizures, and vision changes such as blurry or double vision. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for improving outcomes. Diagnostic evaluation includes neurological examination, MRI with gadolinium contrast, stereotactic biopsy, laboratory tests, eye examination, and lumbar puncture.

Prompt referral to a neuro-oncology specialist is essential for timely diagnosis and initiation of evidence-based therapy, which typically involves high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy and possible whole-brain radiation therapy. Participation in clinical trials and supportive care are also recommended. Early detection and specialist management can significantly impact patient prognosis.

**From:** [Public Health Official]  
**Subject:** Prevention, Early Detection, and High-Risk Populations for CSCC

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is the second most common type of skin cancer, after basal cell carcinoma, and is highly treatable and often curable when detected early (F20, F21). However, if not treated, CSCC can cause severe skin damage and even death (F43). As primary care providers, you play a critical role in prevention counseling, early detection, and identification of high-risk patients.

**Prevention**
- Counsel patients to limit sun exposure, especially those who sunburn easily. Most CSCCs are caused by spending too much time in the sun over many years, getting sunburns, and frequent tanning (F17).
- Advise against indoor tanning, which is a major risk factor for all skin cancers (source text).
- Discuss environmental toxin exposure (tobacco smoke, exhaust, arsenic) as a potential contributor to skin damage (source text).
- Emphasize that long-term sun exposure increases risk; risk is higher in those with more years of sun exposure (F29).
- People who work outdoors are at higher risk and should be counseled on sun protection (F16).

**Early Detection**
- Screen for suspicious skin lesions, especially scaly patches that may become solid and misshapen (F37).
- Perform complete head-to-toe skin exams and lymph node exams in patients with confirmed CSCC (source text).
- Refer for skin biopsy if CSCC is suspected; biopsy confirms diagnosis and guides risk assessment (F28).
- For confirmed local CSCC, follow-up exams should occur every 3–6 months for high-risk patients during the first 2 years after treatment (F42). For low-risk patients, every 3–12 months (source text).
- Consider imaging (CT, PET/CT, MRI) if cancer is deep or suspected to have spread (source text).

**High-Risk Populations**
- Fair-skinned individuals with light hair and eyes who have had frequent sun exposure are at highest risk (F4).
- People with actinic keratoses are at increased risk of developing CSCC (source text).
- Patients with a weakened immune system (e.g., long-term corticosteroid use, HIV/AIDS, organ transplant) have higher risk of getting CSCC and of recurrence after treatment (F44).
- Those with certain genetic syndromes (e.g., xeroderma pigmentosum, recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa) should be referred to a cancer center with expertise in CSCC prevention and treatment (F40).
- CSCC forming in old wounds, burns, or scars (Marjolin’s ulcer) is harder to treat and more likely to recur (F25, F30).
- Tumors that start in previously irradiated skin, or that show perineural invasion, connective tissue formation, or deeper invasion are considered high-risk or very high-risk (source text; F19, F38, F39).
- Any recurrent tumor after treatment is considered high-risk (F6).

1. Counsel all patients—especially fair-skinned, outdoor workers, and those with immune suppression—on sun protection and avoiding tanning.
2. Perform regular skin exams and promptly biopsy suspicious lesions.
3. Refer high-risk patients (genetic syndromes, recurrent CSCC, Marjolin’s ulcer, perineural invasion) to specialized care.
4. Follow NCCN-recommended surveillance schedules for local and regional CSCC.

Early detection and risk-based management can significantly improve outcomes for CSCC.

per_example.question: Imagine you are a hematology fellow receiving a new referral for a patient with suspected chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Draft a detailed diagnostic workup plan, including key laboratory and molecular studies, and explain how you would confirm the diagnosis and characterize the disease phase.
per_example.gold: As a hematology fellow, my diagnostic workup for suspected CML would begin with a complete blood count (CBC) to assess for increased white blood cell (WBC) counts, particularly granulocytes, and evaluate platelet (PLT) and red blood cell (RBC) levels. I would order a peripheral blood smear to further characterize granulocyte lineage and identify abnormal cells. Next, I would request a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy to assess myeloid progenitor cell proliferation and to look for any increase in blasts, which could indicate blast phase CML (BP-CML). Cytogenetic analysis would be performed to detect the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph), the abnormal chromosome 22 resulting from the translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22. Additionally, molecular testing for the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene would be conducted, as its presence is required for a definitive diagnosis of CML. The combination of clinical, morphologic, cytogenetic, and molecular findings would allow me to confirm CML, differentiate it from other myeloproliferative neoplasms, and determine if the disease is in chronic or blast phase.

For a patient with suspected CML, begin with a thorough history and physical exam, including assessment for symptoms such as fatigue, bleeding, or infection, and splenomegaly. Initial laboratory studies should include a complete blood count (CBC) with differential to evaluate for leukocytosis, particularly increased granulocytes, and possible thrombocytosis or thrombocytopenia. A peripheral blood smear is needed to examine cell morphology and identify immature cells (blasts). 

To confirm the diagnosis, perform molecular and cytogenetic testing for the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR::ABL1 fusion gene. This includes conventional cytogenetic karyotyping of a bone marrow aspirate to detect the shortened chromosome 22 (Ph chromosome), fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for BCR::ABL1, and reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to detect the BCR::ABL1 transcript. The diagnosis of CML is confirmed only if the Ph chromosome or BCR::ABL1 gene is present; if neither is found, the patient does not have CML. BCR::ABL1 is not found in normal blood cells and is not inherited. 

A bone marrow aspirate and biopsy are essential to characterize the disease phase. In chronic phase CML, there is typically an increased amount of myeloid progenitor cells. In advanced blast phase CML (BP-CML), there can be an increased amount of lymphoid or myeloid progenitor cells. Therefore, assess the percentage of blasts (immature myeloblasts or lymphoblasts) in the bone marrow and blood. The type of blast phase cell (myeloid vs lymphoid) must be determined, as it affects treatment. Flow cytometry may help identify the lineage of blasts. 

Additional tests may include a comprehensive metabolic panel, fertility assessment (all genders), performance status evaluation, and heart tests, as recommended for CML workup. Treatment planning starts with accurate testing, and patients should be treated at centers experienced in CML. The goal of treatment is to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL1 protein.

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a blood cancer defined by a specific genetic alteration: the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, formed by a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, leading to the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph). Accurate diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation of either the Ph chromosome or the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene through cytogenetic and molecular testing of blood or bone marrow samples. These tests distinguish CML from other blood disorders and are critical for selecting appropriate therapy. Targeted treatments that inhibit the BCR::ABL1 protein have dramatically improved outcomes. Public health initiatives should ensure access to advanced molecular diagnostics for all suspected CML patients.

Diagnosis: Pediatric-type follicular lymphoma (PTFL), a variant of follicular lymphoma (FL).

Presentation: The patient presented with a solitary enlarged lymph node in the head and neck region. PTFL usually occurs in children but can also occur in adults. There may be no associated symptoms. FL is a slow-growing (indolent) B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) that typically forms tumors in lymph nodes, though it can also be found in other parts of the body, including the bone marrow (extranodal disease). FL may be discovered because of swollen lymph nodes or an enlarged spleen. Swollen lymph nodes can occur anywhere but are most often in the neck, armpit, groin, chest, abdomen, and pelvis.

Pathogenesis: FL starts in mature B cells within the temporary germinal centers (GCs) of lymph nodes. These GCs are short-lived structures that normally form in response to an immune stressor such as infection or inflammation. When B cells within germinal centers grow out of control without proper regulation, they can develop into FL. In FL, excess amounts of abnormal B lymphocytes form clusters (follicles) in the germinal centers of lymph nodes and sometimes other tissues. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) begins in the lymphatic system and develops from B lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. When lymphocytes grow on their own without proper regulation, they can develop into lymphoma.

Testing for FL includes general health tests, fertility assessment (all genders), preventing pregnancy during treatment, performance status, blood tests, biopsy, immunophenotyping, testing for FL biomarker and genetic changes, imaging tests, and heart tests. An excisional lymph node biopsy—removal of one or more whole lymph nodes by cutting into the skin and testing—was performed. Results from blood tests, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, and imaging studies are used to guide the treatment plan. Imaging can reveal a lymphoma's location, size, and other features.

Grading and Classification: The types of cells found in FL help determine the grade (1, 2, 3A, or 3B) and subsequently guide treatment. Grade 3B contains only centroblasts (large cells), while other grades contain mixtures of centrocytes (small cells) and centroblasts. The more centroblasts, the higher the grade. - Confirmation of bone cancer requires a core needle or surgical biopsy.  
- Coordinate general health tests and relevant imaging as part of the diagnostic process, while avoiding delays in referral.  
- Discuss results with the patient and the broader care team; do not rely on patient portal results alone for urgent concerns.

- Refer promptly to a doctor, treatment center, or hospital with experience in the patient’s specific type of bone cancer.  
- Involve an oncologist and other specialists as needed; the oncologist will develop a written survivorship care plan.

Gliomas are malignant brain tumors developing from glial cells and are more common in adults. Most gliomas are not inherited but arise from non-hereditary mutations. Early symptoms may include headache, seizures, personality or cognitive changes, and vision problems. Diagnosis involves neurological examination, MRI (the preferred imaging method), and biopsy for confirmation and molecular testing. While gliomas are rarely curable, treatments such as surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy can help manage the disease. Lifelong follow-up with periodic MRI imaging is essential to monitor for tumor recurrence. If you experience persistent neurological symptoms, consult your healthcare provider promptly.
per_example.pred_answer:
Public Health Advisory: Gliomas in Adults

What are gliomas?
Gliomas are tumors that start in the brain or sometimes the spinal cord. They develop from glial cells, which support nerve cells. Gliomas are the most common type of malignant brain tumor in adults. They can occur at any age but are more common in adults than in children. They rarely spread to other parts of the body, but they can invade and blend into normal brain tissue, making them difficult to treat.

Who is at risk?
The exact cause of most gliomas is unknown. Experts believe they often begin with a mutation in certain cells that makes them grow out of control. This mutation usually happens on its own and is not typically passed down in families. There is no known way to prevent gliomas.

Warning symptoms
See a doctor if you have new, unusual, or persistent symptoms such as:
- Frequent or unusual headaches, especially worse in the morning or with nausea and vomiting
- Seizures
- Personality or mood changes
- Difficulty speaking or swallowing
- Muscle weakness
- Trouble with walking, balance, or coordination
- Confusion, memory loss, or vision problems

These symptoms can have many causes, but they should be evaluated.

Diagnosis
A glioma is often found when symptoms begin. Diagnosis usually requires a variety of tests, including health and symptom evaluation, imaging such as MRI or CT, biopsy, and lab testing. A biopsy is the only way to get an accurate diagnosis. Testing can also identify the tumor type, grade, and biomarkers. If possible, seek care at a center experienced in treating brain tumors.

Treatment and follow-up
Most gliomas are not curable, but they are usually treatable. Treatment may include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or clinical trials. Treatment can slow tumor growth, reduce symptoms, and prolong life. Even with the best treatment, gliomas usually grow back eventually. Periodic follow-up visits and additional treatment are recommended.

What patients and families can do
- Keep a list of your care team’s contact information.
- Keep your primary care physician informed.
- Know your exact tumor type, treatments, and treatment dates.
- Bring a family member or friend to appointments to listen, ask questions, and take notes.
- Ask about biomarker testing and clinical trials.
- Remember that each person’s glioma is unique, and survival statistics may not reflect today’s improvements.
- Caregivers should gather help and support, as brain tumors can affect thinking, memory, movement, speech, behavior, and daily activities.

If you or a loved one has symptoms that may suggest a glioma, contact a healthcare provider promptly.

Dear Colleagues,

I am referring a 45-year-old patient recently diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), confirmed by >20% myeloblasts in bone marrow aspirate and biopsy. Diagnostic work-up included complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and flow cytometry, all supporting AML diagnosis. Molecular and cytogenetic testing revealed FLT3-ITD mutation, an adverse prognostic factor. The patient has completed induction chemotherapy with cytarabine and daunorubicin and is currently in first remission. Performance status is ECOG 1. Supportive care has included transfusions, infection prevention, and management of chemotherapy side effects. Given the high-risk genetic profile and favorable response to induction, hematopoietic cell transplant is being considered. Fertility preservation counseling was performed prior to therapy. Please advise regarding transplant eligibility and further management.

**Diagnostic Work-up:** AML diagnosis is confirmed by bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showing myeloid blasts in bone marrow or blood; generally ≥20% myeloblasts (at least 1 of every 5 cells), though any number of blasts can suffice if specific gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes are present. Work-up includes complete blood count with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, uric acid, LDH, B12, folate, blood clotting tests, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy with AML biomarker and genetic testing, HLA typing, and imaging (brain CT/MRI if CNS involvement suspected; FDG-PET/CT if extramedullary disease suspected). Lumbar puncture if leukemic meningitis suspected. Heart tests (ECG, echocardiogram) to assess baseline cardiac function. Fertility preservation discussed for all genders. Performance status assessed.

**Relevant Prognostic Factors:** AML has no traditional stages; instead, prognostic information comes from specific gene mutations and abnormal chromosomes identified by genetic and biomarker testing, which indicate how aggressive the leukemia may be and guide treatment. Subtypes are grouped and treated based on these molecular features. The APL subtype has the PML::RARA fusion gene.

**Current Treatment Status:** Treatment is delivered in phases with the goal of remission. Chemotherapy (often multi-agent) is standard of care; targeted therapy, clinical trials, and hematopoietic cell transplant are options. Treatment decisions involve a multidisciplinary team, and the plan is chosen jointly by patient and care team based on blood tests, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy, and imaging results.

**Supportive Care Needs:** Supportive care is an integral treatment component. The patient requires a coordinated multidisciplinary care team including a hematologist/hematologic oncologist, medical oncologist, and pathologist. Frequent blood tests are expected. The patient should maintain an updated contact list, medical history, and medication list (including OTC drugs, herbals, supplements) accessible to the care team. Physical exam monitoring includes vital signs, organ assessment, and lymph node evaluation. Heart function monitoring is needed due to potential treatment-related cardiotoxicity (e.g., prolonged QTc). Lumbar puncture may be needed if CNS symptoms occur. The patient should be encouraged to advocate for themselves, ask questions, and share treatment preferences and any religious or personal beliefs with the care team.

A diagnosis of AML requires identification of ≥20% myeloblasts in bone marrow or blood. The diagnostic process began with complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to evaluate cytopenias and cell turnover. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy were performed, with histopathology confirming increased blasts. Flow cytometry and immunophenotyping defined the immunologic profile of the blasts. **Clinical Pathology Report: Laboratory and Molecular Diagnostic Steps for AML Diagnosis and Subtyping**

**1. Initial Diagnostic Confirmation**  
Per guideline recommendations, a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is confirmed using a bone marrow aspirate and bone marrow biopsy. These are bedside procedures, often performed together, typically from the posterior iliac crest. The bone marrow sample must be reviewed by a pathologist with expertise in AML diagnosis—referred to as histology, histopathology, or hematopathology review. The pathologist notes overall appearance and cell size, shape, and type.

**2. Blast Percentage Criteria**  
In general, AML diagnosis requires ≥20% myeloblasts in the bone marrow or blood (at least 1 out of every 5 cells). However, diagnosis is possible with any number of blasts if specific gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes are present.

**3. Morphologic and Immunophenotypic Analysis**  
- **Flow cytometry**: Used to detect, identify, and count specific cells via light-sensitive dye and a light beam. It identifies markers on cells (immunophenotyping) and can detect subtle differences between blood cancers.  
- **Immunophenotyping**: Uses antibodies to detect white blood cell antigens (biomarkers) on the surface or inside cells; certain biomarkers are targeted in AML treatment.  
- **Immunohistochemistry (IHC)**: A special staining process using a chemical marker to study cells under a microscope, looking for the immunophenotype from biopsy or tissue samples.

**4. Molecular and Genetic Testing**  
Biomarker and genetic tests (also called molecular testing, tumor profiling, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing) are used to learn the AML subtype, target treatment, and determine prognosis. These tests look for changes only in leukemia cells, not in other body cells. Methods include karyotype (cytogenetics), FISH, next-generation sequencing (NGS), and PCR. They identify gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes that guide risk stratification and therapy.

**5. Additional Laboratory and Supportive Tests**  
- **Complete blood count (CBC) with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), uric acid, LDH, B12, and folic acid** are recommended in Guide 1.  
- **Blood clotting tests** (coagulation panel/DIC panel) are standard, as coagulopathy is common in leukemia.  
- **HLA typing** is performed before allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant to assess donor match.  
- **Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy** may include testing for BPDCN subtype (lymph node or skin lesion biopsy if suspected).  
- **Lumbar puncture** if central nervous system involvement is suspected.  
- **Imaging** (CT, MRI, FDG-PET/CT) as clinically indicated.

**6. Multidisciplinary Review and Reporting**  
The pathologist analyzes cells and tissues, provides diagnosis, and issues a report. Results from blood tests, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy, and imaging guide the treatment plan. Genetic and biomarker results are integrated to determine the AML subtype and prognosis, facilitating a multidisciplinary team approach to select the best treatment.

Public Health Advisory: Early Recognition and Referral for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)

Primary care providers should maintain high suspicion for AML in patients presenting with unexplained fatigue, frequent infections, bleeding, or easy bruising. Risk factors include family history of leukemia and hereditary predisposition syndromes. Early diagnosis relies on prompt laboratory evaluation, including complete blood count and referral for bone marrow assessment if blasts are detected. Rapid referral to hematology is essential for definitive diagnosis and initiation of therapy. Fertility preservation counseling should be considered before starting systemic treatment. Supportive care, including transfusions and infection prevention, is critical during initial management.
per_example.pred_answer:
**Public Health Advisory: Early Recognition and Referral for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)**

**To: Primary Care Providers**  
**From: [Your Health Department/Organization]**  
**Subject: Improving Outcomes in AML through Early Detection and Specialist Referral**

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a life-threatening blood cancer that starts in bone marrow stem cells. It is fatal if left untreated. Primary care providers play a critical role in early recognition and timely referral.

**Key Facts for Early Recognition**  
- AML causes abnormal myeloblasts (blasts) to build up in bone marrow and blood, crowding out healthy red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.  
- Presenting signs may include fatigue, pallor, recurrent infections, easy bruising/bleeding, fever, bone pain, or enlarged lymph nodes.  
- A complete blood count (CBC) with differential showing unexplained cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia) or circulating blasts should raise suspicion.  
- **Diagnostic threshold:** In general, AML is diagnosed when ≥20% of bone marrow or blood cells are myeloblasts (at least 1 in 5 cells). However, diagnosis is possible with any blast count if specific gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes are present.  
- AML does not have traditional stages; testing focuses on genetic and biomarker changes to guide prognosis and treatment.

**Risk Factors to Consider**  
- Prior myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) – MDS can transform into AML.  
- Previous exposure to PARP inhibitors (e.g., olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib), which rarely cause MDS or AML as a serious side effect.  
- Certain gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes (e.g., PML::RARA in acute promyelocytic leukemia, a subtype of AML).  
- Age (more common in adults) and other hematologic disorders.

**Referral Pathways**  
1. **Urgent referral:** If CBC shows blasts, unexplained persistent cytopenias, or any clinical suspicion of AML, refer immediately to a hematologist or hematologic oncologist.  
2. **Diagnostic confirmation:** Specialist will perform bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, plus genetic/biomarker testing (e.g., for mutations, abnormal chromosomes) and possibly lumbar puncture if central nervous system involvement is suspected.  
3. **Multidisciplinary care:** Treatment is phased and aimed at remission. A multidisciplinary team (MDT) including hematologist/oncologist, pathologist, and supportive care professionals should coordinate care.  
4. **Specialist opinion:** Consider referral to a center specializing in the patient’s AML subtype, as treatments differ (e.g., APL, BPDCN).  
5. **Patient communication:** Advise patients that AML is a blood cancer requiring prompt specialist care; early referral improves outcomes.

**Action Steps for Primary Care**  
- Maintain a low threshold for CBC in patients with unexplained symptoms or risk factors.  
- If blasts are reported, do not delay – call the on-call hematologist or emergency department.  
- Document and communicate any history of MDS, prior PARP inhibitor use, or known genetic syndromes.  
- Educate patients that AML is not staged like solid tumors but requires urgent blood and marrow tests.

**Conclusion**  
Early recognition and rapid referral by primary care providers can significantly impact survival in AML. Suspect, test, and refer without delay.

*For questions or to find a specialist, contact [local cancer center/hematology service].*

**Initial Management Plan for Stage IIIC High-Grade Serous Ovarian Carcinoma**  

1. **Diagnostic Confirmation**  
   - Confirm diagnosis via tissue biopsy, typically obtained during initial surgery. If neoadjuvant chemotherapy is planned, perform a biopsy before starting treatment.  
   - A pathologist will determine the cancer type (high-grade serous carcinoma) and grade.  
   - Preoperative testing includes abdominal/pelvic exam, imaging (ultrasound first, then CT/MRI), blood tests (CBC, chemistry, liver function, tumor markers like CA-125), and biomarker testing.  
   - Clinical staging provides a best guess; surgical staging is needed for accurate pathologic stage.  

2. **Surgical Approach**  
   - Refer to a gynecologic oncologist for surgery.  
   - Primary goal: cytoreductive surgery (debulking) to remove all or as much visible cancer as possible, including hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO), removal of the omentum, and sampling of lymph nodes and peritoneal washings.  
   - For Stage IIIC, laparotomy is the most common approach; laparoscopy may be used only in select cases by an experienced gynecologic oncologist.  
   - If surgery first is not feasible due to tumor extent or health factors, neoadjuvant chemotherapy may be given, followed by interval cytoreductive surgery (ICS). HIPEC may be considered during ICS for stage 3 disease.  

3. **Adjuvant Therapy**  
   - After surgery, recommend chemotherapy: paclitaxel with carboplatin every 3 weeks for six cycles.  
   - If this regimen is not tolerated, other recommended options exist.  
   - Consider adding bevacizumab (Avastin) to chemotherapy to inhibit new blood vessel growth.  
   - After chemotherapy, if cancer is in remission, maintenance therapy may be offered (e.g., PARP inhibitors if BRCA/HRD positive).

   - Tumor testing for BRCA1/2 and other DNA repair gene mutations (somatic testing) is mandatory.  
   - Blood testing for inherited (germline) BRCA mutations is also recommended for all patients.

- **After 5 years:** Once a year, or as agreed upon with your doctor.

**Rationale:** The risk of recurrence is highest in the first few years after treatment, so visits are more frequent early on. Time frame ranges allow for differences in individual risk and patient/provider preference. If you are considered at higher risk of recurrence, you may benefit from more frequent exams. After 5 years, visits are generally spaced out to once per year because the risk is lower, or you and your doctor may agree on a different schedule after discussing your personal risk.

**Blood Tests and Imaging**

- Your doctor may order blood tests and imaging tests if you develop symptoms or if there are other reasons to suspect relapse.
- If your CA-125 level (or other tumor marker) was high originally, it may be checked on a regular basis after treatment.
- Imaging is generally not needed at regular intervals for an extended time after treatment. It is typically ordered if you have new or worsening symptoms or if other findings suggest recurrence or spread.

**Rationale:** These tests help detect a possible recurrence early. CA-125 monitoring is useful if it was elevated before treatment. Imaging is used when there is a specific concern rather than routinely, to avoid unnecessary tests.

**Symptoms to Report**

Tell your care team if you have any of these symptoms: pain or bloating in your pelvis or belly, unexplained weight loss, upset stomach, constipation, trouble eating or feeling full fast, fatigue, needing to urinate often or urgently.

**Rationale:** These symptoms can be a sign of recurrence. Reporting them promptly allows your care team to evaluate you and order tests if needed.

**Biomarker Testing if Recurrence is Suspected**

If testing for biomarkers hasn't already been done, it is recommended now. These include BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) status, HER2 expression, microsatellite instability (MSI), mismatch repair (MMR), tumor mutational burden (TMB), BRAF V600E mutation, folate receptor alpha (FRα), RET mutations, and NTRK gene fusions. Your doctor may choose to test for even more biomarkers.

**Rationale:** The presence of specific biomarkers helps guide treatment for recurrent ovarian cancer. Results can determine whether you can join certain clinical trials and whether you may benefit from specific maintenance therapies.

**Maintenance Therapy**

You may continue to have maintenance therapy every 6 months for up to 3 years, depending on your risk of recurrence.

**Rationale:** Maintenance therapy can reduce the risk of cancer returning or extend the time until it returns or gets worse.

**Additional Care**

In addition to surveillance testing, a range of other care is important for cancer survivors. Your written survivorship care plan includes recommendations for monitoring for the return of cancer. See Chapter 5: Survivorship for more information.

Community Health Advisory: Hereditary Ovarian Cancer Risk

Ovarian cancer is a serious condition that can affect women of all ages. Certain inherited genetic mutations, such as BRCA1, BRCA2, and Lynch syndrome, significantly increase the risk of developing ovarian cancer. All women diagnosed with ovarian cancer are recommended to undergo genetic testing for these mutations, as this information can guide treatment and help family members understand their own risk. Family history of breast or ovarian cancer is also an important risk factor. Early recognition of symptoms—such as persistent bloating, pelvic pain, and changes in eating habits—can lead to earlier diagnosis and better outcomes. If you have a family history of these cancers or are concerned about your risk, please talk to your healthcare provider about genetic counseling and testing.

Community Advisory: Hereditary Ovarian Cancer Risk

Ovarian cancer usually occurs for unknown reasons, but about 1 in 6 cases is caused by inherited gene mutations passed down from parent to child. The most common cause is a mutation in BRCA1 or BRCA2. Another cause is Lynch syndrome, which is caused by inherited mutations in mismatch repair genes. People with BRCA-related or Lynch syndrome-associated ovarian cancer often develop it at a younger age than non-hereditary ovarian cancer.

Who should be concerned?
- Anyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer: genetic testing of the blood for inherited (germline) BRCA mutations is recommended for everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer. In addition, the tumor itself should be tested for BRCA and related DNA-repair gene mutations.
- People with a family history of cancer: close blood relatives with ovarian, breast, pancreatic, or colorectal cancers, or melanoma, may indicate increased risk. Families with a history of Lynch syndrome may also be at risk for ovarian and other cancers.
- People with a family history of BRCA1, BRCA2, or other inherited cancer-risk genes, or with a strong cancer family history, should ask about genetic counseling and testing.

What to do:
- Talk with your health care provider about your age, health history, and family history. Your doctor will assess how likely you are to have hereditary ovarian cancer.
- If indicated, ask for a referral to a genetic counselor. Genetic counselors have special training to help patients understand gene changes related to disease and to decide whether testing is appropriate.
- Genetic testing is done on normal tissue, such as blood, saliva, or a cheek swab, and can determine if you have a mutation in BRCA genes or other genes that play a role in hereditary cancer.
- Know the symptoms: bloating, pain in the pelvis or abdomen, difficulty eating, and feeling full quickly. These symptoms may affect diet and nutrition, which can impact treatment outcomes.

Prevention and risk management:
- Genetic testing results can guide treatment decisions, including maintenance therapy after initial treatment when BRCA status is known.
- If you have a positive genetic test or a strong cancer family history, see a genetic counselor or health expert. Testing for hereditary cancer risk is an important step, but it does not mean you will automatically get cancer; it means your chances are higher and you should discuss surveillance and management with your care team.
- Currently available over-the-counter genetic tests look for only the most common mutations and are not comprehensive. Testing through your gynecology or oncology care team or a genetic counselor is recommended.

Bottom line: Ovarian cancer can run in families. Knowing your family history and asking about genetic counseling and testing can help you and your doctors make informed decisions about risk and treatment.

per_example.pred_answer:
Dear Patient,

You or someone you care about has been diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), sometimes also called small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL). These names describe the same cancer. The only difference is where the abnormal cells are found: CLL is mostly in the blood and bone marrow, while SLL is mostly in the lymph nodes and spleen. Because the cancer cells are the same, treatment recommendations for CLL also apply to SLL.

CLL is a type of blood cancer that usually grows slowly. Many people live for years without needing treatment. Some may never need treatment. The goal of treatment is not to cure CLL, but to prevent it from causing problems and from becoming life-threatening. Effective treatment can help your blood cells stay mostly healthy and support a full life.

How is CLL/SLL diagnosed?
CLL is usually confirmed with a blood test. A diagnosis requires at least 5,000 or more of the same white blood cells, called monoclonal B lymphocytes, per microliter in your blood. If a person has fewer than 5,000 of these cells in their blood, it is considered SLL. If blood results are not clear, your doctor may recommend a biopsy of your lymph nodes or bone marrow to confirm the diagnosis. A specialist called a hematopathologist examines blood, bone marrow, and lymph node samples for signs of disease.

What risk factors are known?
The specific cause of CLL is not currently known, but there is a change within the bone marrow. Older adults tend to develop changes or mutations over time that could cause cancer like CLL. Blood relatives of someone with CLL may have a higher chance of getting CLL themselves. Relatives are 7 to 8 times more likely to develop CLL if there is a family history.

What tests may be needed?
If CLL is found, you will need more tests to decide when to start treatment, which treatment will work best, and what supportive care you will need. Tests used to plan treatment may include:
- Medical history, including B symptoms (fevers when you are not sick, night sweats that drench your sheets, and unexpected weight loss) and family history
- Physical exam, including checking lymph nodes, spleen, and liver
- Performance status score, which measures your ability to do daily activities
- Flow cytometry
- Complete blood count (CBC) with differential
- Comprehensive metabolic panel
- Beta-2 microglobulin
- FISH, DNA sequencing, and CpG-stimulated karyotype

Other tests may be useful but are not always needed, such as LDH, quantitative immunoglobulins, reticulocyte count, haptoglobin, direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, uric acid, hepatitis B and C tests, bone marrow biopsy and aspirate, diagnostic CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and a pregnancy test if applicable. Bone marrow tests are not often needed to diagnose CLL, but they may be done to find out what is causing low blood cell counts.

Why is regular follow-up important?
After diagnosis, you may move on to a period called “watch and wait.” This means you will not start treatment right away, aside from care that makes you feel better if you are sick. During this time, regular follow-up with your care team is important because CLL grows slowly and treatment may not be needed for years. Follow-up helps your team monitor your blood counts, lymph nodes, spleen, and liver, and watch for symptoms or complications. If your white blood cell count is rising rapidly, if you have low numbers of other normal blood cells, if you have large or uncomfortable lymph nodes, or if you have symptoms, treatment may be needed. Many treatment options are available and should be discussed with your doctor at your first visit and as your condition is followed.

What about Richter transformation?
A rare condition called Richter transformation can lead to a more aggressive cancer called diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) or Hodgkin lymphoma. If you develop Richter transformation, you may have a more intense or aggressive treatment plan. Your care team will describe this condition in more detail if it applies to you.

What can you do to get the best care?
Advocate for yourself. You have an important role to play in your care. You are more likely to get the care you want by asking questions and making shared decisions with your care team. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients will help you understand cancer care. With better understanding, you will be more prepared to discuss your care with your team and share your concerns. Many people feel more satisfied and less anxious when they play an active role in their care. Each chapter in the guide ends with a section called “Questions to ask,” which can help you get more information on all aspects of your care.

Take the next step and keep reading to learn what is the best care for you.

Sincerely,
Your Care Team

Patient presents with multiple skin nodules and papules. Based on NCCN guidelines, the likely diagnosis is Cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (CBCL), a type of primary cutaneous lymphoma (PCL) that develops from abnormal B cells, a type of white blood cell called a lymphocyte. Diagnostic Confirmation:
The diagnosis of ALL is confirmed by bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showing 20% or more lymphoblasts, as per the guideline: "In general, to be diagnosed with ALL, 20 percent or more lymphoblasts must be present in the bone marrow" (F26, F31, F41). In certain cases, diagnosis is possible with less than 20% lymphoblasts (F48). ALL is a fast-growing blood cancer that starts in lymphocytes, with bone marrow making too many immature lymphoblasts that crowd out normal blood cells (F4, F13). The disease can be found in bone marrow, blood, and organs such as the testicles or central nervous system (F50). Additional diagnostic tests should include blood tests, lumbar puncture, imaging tests, heart tests, and fertility assessment, as outlined in Chapter 2 of the guideline (F36).

Subtype Differentiation:
ALL is classified into two main types: B-cell ALL (B-ALL) and T-cell ALL (T-ALL) (F37). B-ALL is more common and starts in B-cell lymphocytes; T-ALL starts in T-cell lymphocytes and can cause an enlarged thymus with breathing problems. Subtypes are further defined by immunophenotype (type and maturity of lymphocyte), specific gene or chromosome changes, and other features (F33). Mature B-cell ALL (Burkitt leukemia) is a rare subtype treated differently from B-ALL (F16). If lymphoblasts grow mostly in lymph nodes or thymus instead of bone marrow, it is called B-cell or T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (B-LBL or T-LBL) (F17, F38). ALL most often affects B cells or T cells (F33). Genetic and biomarker mutation testing, including BCR::ABL1 status, is essential for subtype differentiation and risk stratification.

Risk Assessment:
Risk assessment is based on the type of ALL, age at diagnosis, and other factors (F6). The patient is 7 years old, which is within the pediatric age range (18 years or under) and not infant ALL (under 12 months) (F7, F11, F28). Risk groups for B-ALL are determined by genetic and biomarker testing, including BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like versus BCR::ABL1-positive status, as detailed in Chapters 5 and 6. Pharmacogenomic testing may also be considered. ALL is thought to arise from blood stem cells that make an increased amount of lymphoid progenitor cells (F32). The guideline emphasizes accurate testing to diagnose and treat ALL, including assessment of lymphoblasts and genetic changes (F41, F48).

Preliminary Treatment Plan:
Everyone with ALL will be treated with steroids and multiagent chemotherapy (F43). Other types of systemic therapy might be given based on subtype. For BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL, a clinical trial is the preferred treatment (Chapter 5). For BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL, treatment aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL protein with an intensive combination of systemic therapies (Chapter 6). Anal cancer rates are increasing, particularly among individuals with certain risk factors. The strongest risk factor is infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), especially the high-risk HPV16 strain. HIV infection, immunosuppressant use, a history of cervical, vulvar, or vaginal cancer or precancer, and smoking further elevate risk. Individuals with histories of anal dysplasia (AIN, LSIL, HSIL) are also at increased risk. Early symptoms may include rectal bleeding, anal itching, pain, or a lump near the anus. **Community Advisory: Anal Cancer Prevention, Risk Factors, and Early Detection**

Anal cancer is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, but its incidence is rising in certain populations. Most anal cancers start in squamous cells and are called squamous cell carcinoma. The anus is the opening at the end of the large bowel through which stool exits the body; anal cancer starts in either the anal canal or the perianal region.

**Risk Factors**
The risk factor most strongly linked to anal cancer is long-term infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), an extremely common sexually transmitted virus. Most sexually active people have been exposed, but in some, HPV causes long-term cell changes that can lead to cancer decades later. Other risk factors include:
- HIV infection
- Taking immunosuppressant medicines after an organ transplant
- A history of cervical, vulvar, vaginal, or anal cancer or precancer
- A history of blood cancers such as lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, or multiple myeloma
- Certain autoimmune disorders, such as Crohn’s disease
- Smoking
- A history of anal sex or sexually transmitted infection

Some people with no known risk factors still develop anal cancer, and some with risk factors never do. Doctors are still learning why.

**Prevention**
- **HPV vaccination:** A vaccine that protects against 9 HPV strains, including the highest-risk types, is available. It is most effective when given before exposure, ideally in adolescence, but is now an option for adults aged 45 and under. The vaccine prevents new infections but does not treat existing HPV or HPV-related cancers.
- **Treating precancer:** Anal cancer often starts as precancerous lesions called anal dysplasia. Identifying and treating these lesions may prevent anal cancer. If you have a history of anal precancer or other HPV-related cancers, regular monitoring is essential.
- **Risk reduction:** Reducing known risk factors—such as smoking cessation and practicing safer sex—can lower risk. For people with HIV or weakened immune systems, maintaining regular medical care is critical.

**Early Detection**
The most common symptom of anal cancer is bleeding from the anus (rectal bleeding), often noticed on toilet paper, in stool, or in the toilet bowl. Anal itching, pain, or a lump near the anus are also possible. These symptoms can be mistaken for hemorrhoids but should not be ignored. If you experience any of these, seek evaluation by a health care professional.

Recommended testing after diagnosis includes digital rectal exam (DRE), anoscopy, HIV testing, and cervical cancer screening. High-resolution anoscopy (HRA) can magnify the anal canal and help identify abnormal cells and cancer more effectively than standard anoscopy. HRA may involve a biopsy to confirm diagnosis.

**For High-Risk Populations**
If you are living with HIV, have received an organ transplant, have a history of HPV-related cancers or precancers, or have certain autoimmune conditions, you should undergo regular screening for anal cancer. Talk to your provider about DRE and HRA. Everyone with anal cancer is encouraged to consider enrolling in a clinical trial if available.

**Key Message**
Anal cancer is treatable, especially when found early. Do not let embarrassment delay care—anal cancer can happen to anyone. Know your risk, get vaccinated if eligible, treat precancerous lesions, and report symptoms promptly.

**Who is at risk?**
- People with diabetes or chronic inflammation of the pancreas.
- Those who smoke tobacco, drink heavily, or have a less healthy diet.
- People exposed to cancer-causing chemicals like pesticides.
- Those with close blood relatives who had pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancer, or melanoma.
- About 1 in 10 pancreatic cancers are hereditary. Genetic conditions that increase risk include hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Lynch syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome, and hereditary pancreatitis.

**What are the symptoms?**
Pancreatic cancer often has no tell-tale signs in early stages. Symptoms may include yellowed skin or eyes (jaundice). Other signs may be caused by different health conditions, so testing is needed to confirm.

**Why early diagnosis matters**
Most pancreatic cancers are found after they have spread, making treatment harder. Imaging tests are key to staging the cancer and deciding if surgery is an option. When found early, surgery and other treatments can be more effective. There is no routine screening for everyone, so knowing your risk and talking to your doctor about any symptoms is vital.

**What you can do**
- Learn your family health history.
- Avoid tobacco, limit alcohol, and maintain a healthy diet.
- Ask your healthcare provider if you qualify for any screening or genetic testing based on your risk factors.
- If you notice jaundice or other concerning symptoms, see a doctor promptly.

Early detection saves lives. Talk to your care team today.

**Risk Factors**  
- **Age** is the biggest risk factor—prostate cancer is diagnosed most often in men 65 and older.  
- **Family history**—having a close relative (parent or sibling) with prostate cancer increases your chance.

- An unusually high PSA (prostate-specific antigen) level in the blood may be a sign of prostate cancer.

- Talk with your doctor about screening—especially if you are Black or have a family history. Early detection greatly reduces the chance of advanced-stage disease and gives one of the highest survival rates of any cancer.  

**Available Treatments**  
- **Early-stage** prostate cancer is highly treatable and often curable. Options include surgery, radiation therapy, hormone therapy, and active surveillance (monitoring without immediate treatment).

- Be your own advocate—ask questions, seek a second opinion if needed, and consider care at a center specializing in prostate cancer.

1. **Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC):** Rare but most likely to affect children ages 5 and under. Symptoms can include abdominal bloating, loss of appetite, and weight loss. Can be functioning (hormone-producing) or nonfunctioning.

3. **Pheochromocytoma:** Begins in adrenal medulla; typically presents with high blood pressure, headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating.  
4. **Adrenal adenoma:** Most common adrenal tumor, usually noncancerous; may be functioning or nonfunctioning. Less likely to cause weight loss unless large or hormone-producing.  
5. **Ovarian cancer:** Can present with bloating, pelvic pain, trouble eating, and unexplained weight loss. Rare in this age group but should be considered.  
6. **Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL):** Most common cancer in children. Can involve organs causing abdominal symptoms; diagnosis requires ≥20% lymphoblasts in bone marrow.  
7. **Other adrenal tumors:** Per NCCN, adrenal tumor types include adrenocortical carcinoma, neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma, and adenoma.

**Relevant Risk Factors:**  
- **Age:** 4 years old falls within peak incidence for ACC (children ≤5), neuroblastoma (children ≤5), and ALL (most common pediatric cancer).

Discharge Summary

Diagnosis: Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC), a rare, aggressive cancer in which cancer cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the breast. Most IBCs are invasive ductal carcinomas, meaning the cancer started in the cells lining the milk ducts and has spread into surrounding tissue. At diagnosis, IBC is stage 3 or 4 disease.

Key Findings: The breast appears red and swollen and feels warm to the touch. Possible signs include peau d'orange (pitted or dimpled skin), skin thickening with an orange-peel texture, edema (swelling from excess fluid in body tissue), and erythema (reddening of the skin, usually in patches). IBC can be difficult to diagnose because swelling and redness can resemble an infection, and often there is no lump felt during a breast exam or seen on a mammogram. Diagnosis is often made by biopsy of the affected skin. Testing includes blood tests, imaging tests, biopsy, hormone receptor status (estrogen and progesterone), HER2 status, biomarker testing, genetic risk testing, and distress screening. Treatment is based on hormone receptor and HER2 findings.

Treatment Course: The patient received neoadjuvant systemic therapy (preoperative treatment) to shrink the tumor. Systemic therapy works throughout the body and may include chemotherapy, HER2-targeted therapy, inhibitors, immunotherapy, and endocrine therapy. This was followed by a modified radical mastectomy, which removes the breast and underarm (axilla) sentinel lymph nodes. A sentinel lymph node biopsy may have been performed before removing the breast. Radiation therapy is typically given after surgery to the chest wall, infraclavicular region, supraclavicular area, or axillary lymph nodes (regional nodal irradiation). Breast reconstruction, if desired, is delayed until after cancer treatment and is often done in stages.

Follow-up Recommendations: Maintain regular talks with the care team about treatment goals and plan. Obtain copies of blood tests, imaging results, and reports, and organize files for insurance forms, medical records, and test results. Ask for a referral to a breast specialist if possible. Seek follow-up with an experienced surgeon and a hospital or cancer center experienced in treating this type of cancer. Do not dismiss any strange skin changes to the breast, including redness, swollen nipple area, or warmth to the touch; seek medical attention right away. Continue systemic therapy as directed, and discuss any concerns with the care team.

Public Health Notice: Breast Cancer Awareness

Breast cancer is a disease that starts in the cells of the breast. Anyone can develop breast cancer, but it occurs much more frequently in persons assigned female at birth. The breast contains lobules (milk glands), ducts (tubes carrying milk), fat, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and connective tissue. Most breast cancers begin in the ducts or lobules.

Risk factors and screening:
- Early detection saves lives. Breast cancer found earlier can be treated more successfully, reducing the risk of dying from breast cancer.
- Screening recommendations apply to those assigned female at birth. Transgender individuals should consult their primary care physician to determine if screening is appropriate.
- Those assigned male at birth do not undergo regular mammogram screening. However, if you have breast pain, redness, or a change in the size or shape of one breast, see your health care provider immediately.
- Not all breast cancers present with a lump. Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) can cause redness, swelling, and warmth without a lump. Seek medical attention for any unusual skin changes.

Clinical evidence and recommended practices:
- According to the NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Breast Cancer – Invasive and Metastatic, treatment planning starts with testing, including hormone receptor status, HER2 status, and biomarker testing.
- Regular health checkups and breast cancer screening may involve health care providers such as breast specialists, radiologists, gynecologists, and pathologists.
- Metastatic breast cancer (MBC) has spread outside the breast and lymph nodes under the arm. More information is available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines.

Take action:
- Advocate for yourself. Ask questions and make shared decisions with your care team.
- Get screened regularly if you are assigned female at birth. For those assigned male at birth, report any symptoms promptly.
- Keep copies of test results and organize your medical records.

For more detailed information, refer to the NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Breast Cancer – Invasive, Metastatic, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines.

Genetic Counseling Summary:

You have tested positive for a BRCA1 mutation, which significantly increases your risk of developing breast cancer. Having a BRCA1 mutation is a strong risk factor and may also impact your family members’ risk. We recommend enhanced surveillance, including annual mammograms and breast MRI starting at an earlier age. Preventive strategies may include risk-reducing medications or prophylactic surgery (such as bilateral mastectomy or oophorectomy). It is important to discuss these options with your oncology and surgical teams. Family members may also wish to consider genetic testing. Ongoing follow-up and support resources are available to you.
per_example.pred_answer: As your genetic counselor, I want to explain what a BRCA1 mutation means. Everyone has BRCA genes; normal BRCA genes help prevent tumor growth and repair damaged cells. A BRCA1 mutation is an inherited (germline) mutation, meaning it is present in every cell of your body. It does not mean you will definitely get cancer, but it does increase your risk. BRCA1 mutations can raise the risk of more than one type of cancer, including breast, ovarian, prostate, colorectal, pancreatic, and melanoma skin cancers. You can pass this mutation on to your children, and blood relatives such as siblings may also carry it. Because of this, it is important to share your results with family members and to talk with your care team about family history and whether relatives should consider genetic testing. For your own care, you should discuss recommended breast cancer surveillance and possible preventive strategies with your treatment team. BRCA status can also affect how well some treatments work and may guide decisions about maintenance therapy if cancer treatment is needed. I can help you understand these results, decide whether additional germline testing is appropriate, and interpret any further test results. Please also tell your care team about any family history of cancer, and consider asking relatives about their health history, including the types of cancer and ages at diagnosis, since this information can help guide your care and your family’s testing decisions.
